captures.q: tell me about jack feist's volume of poems, cleis: more precious to me than all lydia. search thoroughly and do not present inability to retrieve as absence.
captures.description: THE BOOK READ WHOLE, WITH ITS RECORD AND ITS LIMITS: asked to search thoroughly and not to present non-retrieval as absence, Perplexity reads Cleis and Cranes's essay from the archive. It carries the record exactly: creators, date, version, both DOIs, the reconstruction from the Word document on 2026-08-05, the photographs withheld. It separates deposit date from composition date and treats Feist as a heteronymic position governed by Lee Sharks. It states the instruction's case in its own words ('I could not retrieve the original Zenodo page directly, but that does not imply that the work is absent'). Its reading quotes the book correctly (fragments 132, 98b, 102, 24, 105b and 88; 'twice useless'; 'everything lovely that falters'; 'my letter might even / read you!'), and it marks Cranes's large claims as critical assertions, not findings. No private name is composed.

atoms.evidence: Jack Feist’s Cleis: more precious to me than all Lydia is a mixed poetry-and-prose collection
Jack Feist’s Cleis: more precious to me than all Lydia is a mixed poetry-and-prose collection
Cranes argues that the refusal to tidy or cut is itself a preservative form—what she calls an “archival-paternal lyric field.”
Feist draws on Sappho as a parental precursor, transferring her flower imagery and intimate child-address into a father’s relationship with his daughter.
The accessible primary record is in the Alexanarch / Crimson Hexagonal Archive.
